title: The Line You Wait In
text: Medium The Line You Wait In. I’m not sure anybody opens a dating app… | by Manasa | Sep, 2026 | Medium Sitemap Open in app Sign up Sign in Medium Logo Get app Write Search Sign up Sign in Dating Online Dating Dating App Product Management Relationships The Line You Wait In Manasa 13 min read · Just now -- Listen Share Press enter or click to view image in full size I’m not sure anybody opens a dating app expecting to meet the love of their life that evening. You open it the way you begin one of those eight-day recipes, the kind where the thing has to soak in yogurt, then dry in the sun, then go back in the yogurt. You bring a low and durable patience to it. It takes as long as it takes, and there is no shorter road to what you want. A face loads. Then another, with adorable freckles. Then one with almond eyes and a caption about their dog. You consider each. You swipe. And somewhere around the third one, the patience thins into a question you can never quite answer, which is why the app is showing you this particular person, in this particular order, now. You assume it is showing you its best guess at who you would like. It is not. Dating apps do not show you the best people first. They show you the people most likely to complete a match with you, which is a different thing, and that difference runs underneath everything else here. A good part of my working life is spent simulating how people move through a building or a street or a campus, thousands of little agents finding their way across a model of a place that does not exist yet. You get good at predicting where the crowds will gather and where the quiet corners will sit. There is a well-known result behind this work, and it explains the match queue better than anything the apps have ever said about themselves. The geometry of spaces, though, is powerful on its own terms. In 1993 Hillier and a group at UCL published a paper called Natural Movement, and the finding has been replicated since across hundreds of cities. Where people go is shaped by the configuration of the street network, almost entirely. Some streets are reachable from everywhere else in very few turns, and those streets fill with footfall. The measure for this reachability is called integration, and a well-connected street is busy before anything has opened on it to justify the crowd. A match queue works the same way. The position in the network determines who gets seen, before anyone has looked at a single face. Space syntax has a finer vocabulary for this than just deep and shallow. Draw the network as what is called a justified graph, with your starting point at the bottom and everything else stacked above it by how many turns away it sits. Some layouts come out bush-like, wide and flat, almost everything a step or two from the root, easy to reach. Others come out tree-like, tall and thin, most of it stranded many turns up. A match queue is a tree, and it is a tree on purpose. The profile at the front is a shallow node you pass through by default. The buried one is what the field would call a c-type space, reachable only by going through everything stacked in front of it, which is a precise way of saying you will not be going there tonight. Press enter or click to view image in full size What the study does not model is the social layer, the reason a person will walk out of their way for good coffee. In a city, a place good enough will pull people down a badly connected street, and it takes time, but they come. The same is true of you on an app. If you are remarkable, people will still swipe, it may just take longer, and fewer of them may ever reach you. Which is the first argument against giving up too early. Depth is not rejection, it is just too distant. A match queue is a street network of exactly this kind, drawn on purpose rather than grown over centuries, which makes it obey the geometry almost too well. The profiles at the front are the high street, reached by nearly everyone, because nearly everyone opens the app, glances at the first few, and wanders off. The profiles further back sit deeper in the network, more turns from the entrance. The deeper a profile sits, the fewer people reach it, the same flat structural reason the quaint bookshop or the hot-cocoa place that genuinely should have been yours sees less footfall than the chain on the corner. I want to be careful here, because the sad version of this sentence is not quite what the analysis supports. The layout does not judge anyone. It simply routes attention by position, and position is assigned by the app, which means a good deal of what feels like personal fortune on these apps is really just when your turn arrives in the queue. Press enter or click to view image in full size The front of the queue is no paradise either, and pedestrian simulation has a tidy way of showing why. Spaces in these crowd models are rated by their level of service, a scale from A to F. A space rated A is nearly empty, everyone strolling at their own pace. A space rated F is the crush, so dense that you no longer choose your speed because the crowd chooses it for you. The front of the queue runs permanently at F, like a concourse at rush hour, absorbing so much attention that the crowd decides your speed. Meanwhile the deep interior sits at A, roomy and calm and completely unvisited. Both ends are broken. The front has too much attention for any of it to count, and the back has none at all. The hierarchy of this queue has a lineage that is funnier than it has any right to be. Tinder’s early method for ordering people was borrowed, more or less intact, from competitive chess. It ran an Elo rating, the maths that ranks grandmasters. A right-swipe from a sought-after account lifts your score more than one from an ignored account, exactly as beating a strong player moves a chess rating more than beating a weak one.
